criterion_notes.c1: Examines household drinking water supply (local utility PDAM connections and shallow wells) and sanitation/wastewater management (household sanitation access, septic tanks, centralized WTP, and untreated river discharge) as two of seven slum indicators in Urban Kampong Pasirjaya, Bogor.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain/literal wording of Criterion 2 because it examines participatory planning governance in slum settlement upgrading (evaluated via Arnstein's Ladder of Citizen Participation and benchmarked against Law No. 25 of 2004, Government Regulation No. 68 of 2010, and PUPR Ministerial Regulation No. 14 of 2018). Fails the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2 because it focuses on generic community participation in landscape and slum-upgrading project planning and cites sectoral regulations only as normative physical standards, without examining any rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, tenure/documentation requirements for connection, tariff rules, enforcement, discretion, or utility regulatory structure) directly governing household water or sanitation service access. Land tenure disputes are mentioned only briefly in relation to public open space development, not water or sanitation access.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical data collected from June to September 2025 via in-depth interviews, focus group discussions (FGDs), participatory mapping, and a 113-item semi-open/open-ended questionnaire with 16 purposively sampled informants, supplemented by secondary Detailed Engineering Design (DED) documents.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports descriptive household service access and expenditure outcomes, including adequate sanitation access (12 of 16 respondents with adequate access, 4 without), reliance on PDAM piped water (15 of 16 respondents) and wells (16 of 16), monthly PDAM water bills (IDR 50,000 to IDR 100,000), and domestic wastewater disposal practices.
criterion_notes.c5: Identifies the study population and sample (16 RT/RW and community leaders from RW 06, RW 07, and RW 12 in Pasirjaya Sub-district, West Bogor, Indonesia), study design (descriptive qualitative case study with participatory planning approach), general participatory governance factor, and descriptive water/sanitation access outcomes, though no rule-type legal/administrative exposure governing WASH access is analysed.

evidence_quotes.quote: Based on Figure 9, the majority of respondents (15 out of 16) rely on the local water utility (PDAM) as their main source of drinking water.
In terms of sanitation, 12 respondents have adequate access, while 4 others do not.
Based on Figure 13, the questionnaire results show that most respondents (16 people) reported that they dispose of domestic wastewater either directly into nearby rivers or by using septic tanks.

This study examines the physical conditions of slum settlements and the level of community participation in the Urban Kampong of Pasirjaya, West Bogor, using a descriptive qualitative method and a participatory planning approach with a landscape planning perspective.

The results of the questionnaire analysis reveal that community participation in Pasirjaya Urban Kampong remains at the levels of Participation through Consultation, Placation, and Partnership, based on Arnstein’s Ladder of Citizen Participation.

In this study, a total of 16 respondents participated in the in-depth interviews and focus group discussions (FGDs). The informants consisted of RT and RW leaders as well as community leaders representing RW 06, RW 07, and RW 12, which have been designated as light slum areas in Pasirjaya Sub-district, Bogor City.

raw_response.exposure: Community participation levels (Consultation, Placation, Partnership on Arnstein's Ladder) in participatory slum settlement and landscape upgrading planning; no rule-type legal or administrative mechanism governing water or sanitation access is examined.
raw_response.outcome: Descriptive slum settlement conditions across seven Permen PUPR No. 14/2018 indicators, including household drinking water source (PDAM utility supply and shallow wells), monthly water expenditure (IDR 50,000-100,000), adequate sanitation access, and domestic wastewater disposal practices.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Urban slum settlement of Pasirjaya Sub-district (RW 06, RW 07, and RW 12; 11.99 hectares), West Bogor District, Bogor City, Indonesia; purposive sample of 16 key informants (RT leaders, RW leaders, and community leaders).
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 rule-type clarification of Criterion 2. Although the study collects primary empirical data reporting household drinking water (PDAM and well use, monthly water spending) and sanitation/wastewater conditions in an urban kampong in Bogor, Indonesia, its governance analysis focuses solely on general community participation in neighborhood slum-upgrading and landscape planning (using Arnstein's Ladder) and cites national housing/water regulations only as descriptive physical benchmarks. It does not examine any legal, administrative, or regulatory rule-type mechanism (such as eligibility rules, tenure/documentation requirements, administrative burden, tariff/cost-recovery rules, enforcement, or utility governance structure) directly governing water or sanitation service access. Under the literal/plain broad wording of Criterion 2, it would be included as an empirical study examining participatory planning governance alongside slum water and sanitation conditions.
raw_response.study_design: Descriptive qualitative case study using semi-open questionnaires (113 items), in-depth interviews, focus group discussions, and participatory mapping
